text: I started running at 38, mostly because my doctor looked at my numbers and sighed. The first month was miserable. My knees ached, I wheezed after two blocks, and I quit twice. What kept me going was a neighbour who simply knocked on my door at 6:30 every morning. Eight months later I ran a 10k. Not fast, but I finished, and I still hear that knock in my head.

Interest rates went up again, and suddenly everybody's a mortgage expert. Here's what I actually saw at our branch: people who'd fixed early were fine, people on variable deals panicked, and a surprising number just waited. Waiting wasn't crazy. Prices in our area barely moved for a year. But I wouldn't call it a strategy either, more like hoping.

Our team went fully remote in 2020 and never came back. Meetings got shorter, which was great. Hallway chat vanished, which was not. We now run a weekly 'nothing agenda' call where people just talk. It sounds silly. Attendance is the highest of anything we do, and two of our best product ideas came out of it.

The Roman roads are famous, but the real trick was maintenance. A road with no one fixing potholes is a rumour of a road. Local towns were assigned stretches and could be fined if theirs crumbled. That's why some of them are still walkable after nearly two thousand years, while a lot of newer asphalt gives up in ten.

Sleep advice usually reads like a checklist you're failing. Mine finally improved when I stopped chasing eight hours and fixed one thing: the phone stays out of the bedroom. That's it. Some nights are still bad. But I fall asleep faster, and I stopped dreading the alarm, which turned out to matter more than the number.

Teaching fractions to ten-year-olds taught me that they don't hate maths, they hate being stuck in public. Give them a pizza, a knife, and permission to be wrong, and half the room comes alive. The other half wants the pizza. Fair enough. I now keep a spare one on the schedule for Fridays.
